title: LibreOffice Restricts LLM Use in Development Process
summary: The Document Foundation implements stricter LLM usage guidelines for LibreOffice contributors, requiring human review and disclosure for all AI-generated code.
body_markdown:
#### 💡 TL;DR


- The Document Foundation rolled out stricter LLM guidelines for LibreOffice contributors on November 24, 2026, requiring full disclosure and human review.
- All AI-generated code submissions must now include explicit documentation of which tools were used and how output was validated.
- The policy aims to maintain code quality, preserve contributor skill development, and ensure legal compliance in the open-source codebase.


The Document Foundation has introduced more restrictive guidelines governing how contributors can use large language models in LibreOffice development. Officially launched on November 24, 2026, the updated policy requires explicit disclosure and human validation for all AI-generated code submissions, marking a significant tightening of the project's stance on automated coding assistance.


## What Changed in the New Policy


The revised guidelines mandate that any contributor using LLMs to generate code, documentation, or commit messages must clearly document which tools were employed and how the output was reviewed. Contributors must demonstrate they understand the generated code rather than blindly accepting AI suggestions. The policy explicitly prohibits submitting AI output without thorough human review and modification.


Key restrictions include a requirement that contributors retain full responsibility for all submitted code, regardless of its origin. The Foundation emphasizes that LLM-generated contributions must meet the same quality standards as human-written code, with particular attention to licensing compatibility and intellectual property concerns inherent in training data provenance.


## Rationale Behind the Restrictions


The Document Foundation cited three primary motivations for the stricter stance. First, maintaining code quality and architectural coherence across a complex codebase that spans millions of lines requires deep contextual understanding that current LLMs often lack. Second, the organization wants to preserve skill development among contributors, particularly newer developers who might become overly reliant on AI assistance.


Third, legal and licensing concerns remain unresolved in the broader software industry. The Foundation noted that uncertainty around training data sources and potential copyright issues creates risk for open-source projects that must maintain clear intellectual property chains. The policy positions LibreOffice conservatively until these legal questions achieve greater clarity.


## Impact on the Contributor Community


The new guidelines represent a contrast to some commercial software projects that have embraced AI coding assistants more enthusiastically. LibreOffice maintainers acknowledged that the restrictions may slow certain development tasks but argued the trade-off protects long-term project health. Contributors who previously used LLMs for routine tasks like boilerplate generation or documentation drafting will now need to invest more manual effort.


The policy does not ban LLM usage entirely. Contributors can still use AI tools for research, learning, or generating initial drafts, provided they thoroughly understand and validate the output before submission. The Foundation emphasized this represents a middle path between outright prohibition and unrestricted use.


## What This Means


LibreOffice's updated[AI usage policy](https://emergent.sh/glossary/ai-usage-policy) reflects growing awareness in open-source communities about the trade-offs of LLM-assisted development. While commercial entities race to integrate AI coding tools, volunteer-driven projects face distinct pressures around legal liability, educational mission, and community governance. The Document Foundation's conservative approach may influence other open-source projects wrestling with similar questions as LLM adoption accelerates across software engineering. Organizations evaluating their own AI development policies will likely watch how this framework performs in practice over the coming months.
